walkthroughs.h2: From the August Revolution to Geneva
walkthroughs.body_html: Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945, citing the American Declaration of Independence. French attempts at recolonisation triggered the First Indochina War (1946-54), ending in the defeat at Dien Bien Phu and the Geneva Accords, which split Vietnam at the 17th parallel.

The cancellation of promised elections, the Diem regime in the South and an emerging National Liberation Front (NLF, or 'Viet Cong') drew the United States deeper into the conflict. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) escalated commitments; by 1968 over 500,000 US troops were deployed. The Tet Offensive (January 1968) undermined American claims of imminent victory.

President Nixon's policy of Vietnamization and the Paris Peace Accords (1973) led to US withdrawal. Without American air power, the South collapsed; North Vietnamese tanks entered Saigon on 30 April 1975. Vietnam was reunified the following year. The war cost up to 3 million Vietnamese lives and over 58,000 American.
